titleDv: ޤާނޫނު ނަންބަރު 12/2016 (ޖިނާއީ އިޖުރާއަތުގެ ޤާނޫނު) އަށް ... ވަނަ އިޞްލާޙު ގެނައުމުގެ ބިލު
summary: This government bill amends the Criminal Procedure Act (Law No. 12/2016) in three main areas. First, it rewrites the rules on bail: who has a right to ask for it, what courts must weigh before granting it, and new rules for bail after conviction but before sentencing, and while an appeal is pending. Second, it lets police intercept phone, electronic and postal communications with a court order in serious crime cases, and adds new powers to investigate cybercrime and collect computer data. Third, it rewrites the appeals chapter, setting out what can be appealed, the deadlines for the High Court and Supreme Court, and how appeals are filed and accepted. The law would take effect three months after it is published in the Government Gazette.
whyItMatters: Telecom and internet companies would have to keep customer details and records of who contacted whom for at least 12 months, and police could get them, or listen in on communications, with a court order. People charged or convicted would face new rules on getting bail and new appeal deadlines, and filing an appeal would no longer pause a sentence.
keyProvisions: Bail (Articles 60, 61, 61-1, 62, 65, 66-1, 68): the bill adds 'may commit another offence' as a ground for keeping a suspect in custody. Before granting bail, courts must weigh past breaches of bail, delays to trial, risk to victims of violent crime and the risk of fleeing. Bail conditions must be reasonable and linked to the case. A person found guilty but not yet sentenced can get bail only if they prove it is needed in the interests of justice. Courts can take passports or ban travel abroad or to another island.

Interception (Article 74): with a court order, police can intercept postal and electronic communications when investigating murder, organised serious crime, terrorism, money laundering and terrorist financing, human trafficking, drug trafficking, national security offences, child sexual abuse, and offences under Article 246 of the Penal Code. The current law only lets police suspend such communications. The application must name the person or device and the suspected crime. Each order lasts up to 90 days, can be renewed 90 days at a time, and what is collected cannot be disclosed.

Data retention (Article 74-1): internet and telecom providers in the Maldives must keep subscriber information and traffic data (who communicated with whom, when, for how long and from where) for at least 12 months. They do not have to keep the content of communications.

Cybercrime powers (Articles 74-2 to 74-6): police can order anyone to quickly preserve computer data, for up to 90 days at a time. Courts can order people or service providers, including foreign providers serving the Maldives, to hand over data, and must decide urgent requests within 24 hours. Courts can also authorise searching and seizing computers and storage, and collecting traffic data in real time for up to 90 days at a time. There are extra protections for legal, medical, religious, banking and other privileged information.

Appeals (Articles 198 to 198-6): the bill lists what can be appealed: verdicts, court orders and pre-trial decisions. Appeals must show a breach of the Constitution, the law or Sharia principles that affected the outcome. Verdicts can be appealed within 60 days, or 75 days for a good reason. Orders and pre-trial decisions must be appealed within 10 days (3 working days for a state appeal to the High Court, 7 for the Supreme Court), and the court must rule within 14 days. Courts must decide within 7 days whether to accept an appeal. Under new Article 198-1, filing an appeal does not delay a sentence being carried out.

Appeals and custody (Articles 199, 201-1, 203): if the accused is charged with a serious offence under Article 22, the Prosecutor General can ask the High Court to keep them in custody or ban their travel until the appeal ends. New Article 201-1 lets people sentenced to jail ask for bail while they appeal, except for Article 63 offences. Article 203 is repealed.
whoIsAffected: People arrested, charged or convicted of crimes, the police, prosecutors and courts, and telecom and internet service providers.
statedReasons: The government says cybercrime is rising in the Maldives and law enforcement lacks the powers it needs to investigate it and collect electronic evidence, so it is adding procedures for data retention, preservation, production orders, search and seizure of computer data, and real-time traffic data. It also proposes changes to court procedure on detention, bail and appeals.
